rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window while minimizing risk of missing late compounds. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, spread across the gradient, or still retained into the hold.

All pairs are vastly over-resolved, so now optimize time by trimming the gradient to the observed elution window and shortening it substantially. The estimated elution range is roughly 0.18 to 0.50 organic, so 0.10–0.70 over 10 min should keep all peaks in-gradient while pulling the last peak much earlier.

We already have full resolution with margin, so push for a sub-10 min last peak by making the gradient slightly steeper and raising temperature one step. The window still covers the apparent elution region, and the large current resolution reserve should tolerate this compression.

Since we have perfect CRF with ample resolution margin, the next step is to shorten the gradient further while holding the successful window and temperature constant. This tests how much faster we can go before the first critical pair approaches the 1.5 resolution threshold or the last peak crosses 10 min.

Resolution is still comfortably above threshold, especially for the limiting first pair, so compress the gradient again to find the speed limit. Keeping the same phi window isolates the effect of slope and should reveal whether we can maintain full-credit resolution at even shorter run time.

At 4 min the worst-pair resolution is still 2.19, so one more step shorter directly tests whether the minimum allowed gradient can still keep every pair at full credit. This is the fastest possible tG, and if it holds, we can then fine-tune temperature or the window only if needed.

The 2 min gradient over-compressed the critical first pair, while 4 min at 45 C was fully resolved, so keep tG at 4 min and raise temperature one step to check whether we can gain speed margin elsewhere without losing full-credit resolution. This probes whether the close pair is temperature-sensitive enough to improve or at least remain acceptable under a hotter, potentially faster condition.

The limiting pair is still the first two peaks, so lowering phi0 should give them more early-gradient space and may recover resolution margin while keeping the run short. With all compounds already eluting well before the end, widening only at the low-organic end is a targeted selectivity test rather than a risk for late elution.

Now tighten the high-organic end, since the last peak is still very early and reducing phi1 can improve use of the gradient window without sacrificing speed. This should test whether the current excess late-gradient strength is unnecessary while preserving full resolution of the critical early pair.

The narrower 0.10–0.60 window improved the limiting pair at 4 min, so retry the minimum 2 min gradient under this better window and hotter temperature. This directly tests whether we can reach the absolute fastest allowed method while keeping the first pair at or above 1.5 resolution.

The 0.10–0.60, 4 min method has full credit with the best resolution margin among the fast runs, so trim phi1 one more step to see if a narrower window further boosts the critical first-pair resolution while keeping all compounds comfortably before 10 min. This is a controlled refinement around the apparent optimum rather than pushing back to the failed 2 min regime.

The 0.10–0.60, 4 min method looks like the best balance so far, so raise temperature one more step to reduce retention while checking whether the critical first pair remains above 1.5. This may deliver the shortest fully resolved run among the 4 min gradients.

At 55 C the 0.10–0.60 method is still fully resolved but the critical pair is close to the 1.5 limit, so narrowing the gradient window slightly should recover some resolution while likely keeping the last peak under 10 min. This tests whether 55 C can be made robust enough to match or beat the fastest full-resolution conditions.

A final temperature step will map the edge of robustness for the fast 0.10–0.60, 4 min window. Since 55 C is just above the 1.5 threshold for the critical pair, 60 C will show whether even higher temperature preserves full resolution or crosses the limit.

The critical first pair is temperature-limited at 55–60 C, so lower phi0 one step while keeping the otherwise attractive 0.60 upper limit and 55 C to see if early selectivity can be improved without sacrificing a short last-peak time. This is a focused attempt to get more margin than the 0.10–0.60, 4 min, 55 C method.

At 55 C the 0.10–0.60 window is right on the edge, so widen the upper end back to 0.65 to slightly reduce gradient steepness and recover robustness for the critical first pair. This checks whether a faster high-temperature method can match the safer 50 C conditions while staying comfortably above the 1.5 threshold.

The close first pair is the limiting factor at 55 C, so lengthen tG to 6 min while keeping the promising 0.10–0.60 window to restore slope-based resolution without any risk of a time penalty. This tests whether 55 C can deliver full robustness at a still-short run time comparable to the 45 C, 4 min method.

The best fast 4 min methods are already fully resolving, and 6 min at 55 C restored ample margin, so drop temperature to 50 C at the same 0.10–0.60, 6 min settings to map the tradeoff between selectivity margin and retention in this narrower window. This gives a cleaner comparison against the successful 4 min and 55 C results without repeating any prior method.

We have many CRF-1.000 methods, so now probe whether the lower-end window can be tightened to further shorten the earliest retention without losing the critical first-pair resolution. Raising phi0 one step at the strong 0.10–0.60, 4 min, 50 C condition directly tests if the first pair depends on very low starting organic or if some dead early time can be removed.

The 0.15–0.60, 4 min, 50 C run retains full-credit resolution with a healthy 1.93 margin on the critical pair, so test whether this tighter low-end window can succeed at the minimum 2 min gradient where broader windows failed. This is the most plausible remaining route to an even faster fully resolved method.

The 2 min gradient consistently fails on the first pair, so continue optimizing within the 4 min family by increasing phi0 one more step to see whether the early pair benefits from a later, tighter low-end window. This may reveal a slightly better balanced fast method while all compounds still elute comfortably before 10 min.

The first peak is now approaching the unretained region at phi0 0.20, but the first pair still has full-credit resolution, so one more phi0 increase will test the practical upper limit of low-end trimming. This helps bracket the fastest robust 4 min window before early compression becomes unacceptable.

The sweet spot appears to lie between phi0 0.15–0.20 and phi1 0.55–0.60 at 4 min, 50 C, so combine the tighter low and high ends to test a more focused gradient window. This may preserve full-credit resolution while reducing unnecessary gradient span better than any single-ended adjustment tested so far.

The best practical region is still 4 min at 50 C, and phi0 = 0.20 gave the shortest-looking early spacing while keeping full resolution, so widen phi1 to 0.65 to slightly ease gradient steepness and test whether that restores extra margin for the first pair without hurting speed too much. This brackets the opposite corner from the failed 0.25–0.60 condition.

The latest run gives the shortest fully resolved last peak so far, and with one injection left the best use is to add robustness by lowering temperature one step at the same fast window and slope. This tests whether the apparent optimum remains fully resolved with a bit more margin on the critical first pair while likely staying well under 10 min.
